Quiz – excavation support walls
At what spacing are the steel I-beams of a soldier pile wall usually placed?
every 0,5–1 m
every 1–3 m, usually 2 m
every 4–6 m
always exactly 3 m apart
1–3 m apart, usually 2 m; a closer spacing can be justified by a higher load.
Why are the soldiers of a soldier pile wall now usually set in bores (rather than driven)?
Because this makes the wall watertight
For noise reasons – and so layers that are hard to drive through are not a problem either
Because no embedment is needed in a bore
Because then no lagging is needed
Noise control, and avoiding layers that are hard to drive through. The bore has to be properly filled – especially below excavation level.
What spacing ensures the watertightness of a jet grout wall?
10–20 cm larger than the diameter
Equal to the diameter
10–20 cm smaller than the diameter
Half the diameter
A spacing 10–20 cm smaller than the diameter gives the overlap – so a quasi-watertight wall can be made.
Why is the size of the steel member that can be placed in a jet grout wall limited?
Because the jetted soil is a very dense fluid until it sets – only the zone of about 15–20 cm around the drilling axis will accept it
Because the diameter of a jet column is at most 30 cm
Because steel corrodes in cement
Because the standard forbids large sections
The vertical line passed through by the drill rod and its 15–20 cm surroundings can accept the steel member – whatever the size of the column.
What gives the reinforced self-hardening slurry wall its watertightness, and what its resistance?
The concrete gives both
The watertightness comes from the hardened slurry, the resistance from the steel sections placed every 1–2 m
The watertightness comes from the steel, the resistance from the slurry
The watertightness comes from a membrane, the resistance from anchors
The cement-bearing slurry becomes watertight when it hardens, but its strength is only 0,5–1,4 MPa – by arching it transfers the load to the steel sections.
Which statement is true of the steel sheet pile wall?
It can only be used as a permanent structure
Thanks to its interlocks it can be watertight, and as a temporary wall it can be extracted and reused
It can only be installed by pressing
Its vibration reaches at most 2–3 m
Thanks to the interlocks it is watertight and can be temporary or permanent; the vibration of driving can reach as far as 20–30 m.
Where is the interlock in a wall made of U (Larssen) sheet piles?
On the outer flanges
In the centre plane of the wall, on the neutral axis
In the middle of the web, on the face of the wall
There is no interlock, they are welded
In U piles the interlock is on the neutral axis (that is why double piles are crimped), in Z piles on the outer flanges.
What is the typical size of the gap between piles in a spaced pile wall?
20–60 cm, but at most the pile diameter
exactly twice the pile diameter
The acceptable gap depends on the stability of the soil and its ability to arch: typically 20–60 cm, at most D.
In a secant pile wall, which piles are made first?
The reinforced piles
The unreinforced (primary) piles, then the reinforced ones between them, cutting about 10–12 cm into them
It does not matter, in any order
The capping beam first
First the unreinforced piles, then between them – cutting about 10–12 cm into them – the reinforced piles that can also take moment. Only every second one is reinforced.
Which wall is NOT suitable as a watertight support for an excavation below the groundwater?
Water seeps through between the planks of a soldier pile wall – it can only be used above the groundwater or with dewatering.
